# Pricing Architecture for Services Firms

Source: https://lowob.com/research/pricing-architecture-for-services-firms/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-14 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Price is the largest profit lever most services firms have and the one they manage least. A pricing architecture is the set of rules that turns a rate card into the fee a firm actually keeps: the fee model, the packages, the discount and exception rules, scope change terms and payment terms. This piece sets out each element, shows where a typical engagement leaks value between list and pocket, and explains why every price exception should be recorded with a reason and an outcome.

A pricing architecture is the set of rules that turns a firm's rate card into the fee it actually keeps: the fee model, the packages, the discount and exception rules, the scope change terms and the payment terms. Most services firms have a rate card and no architecture, so the realised price is set deal by deal. That matters because price is the strongest profit lever available. Marn and Rosiello's classic *Harvard Business Review* analysis found a 1% price improvement, with volume unchanged, lifted operating profit by 11.1%, against 3.3% for a 1% volume gain. Design the architecture once, measure the gap between list and pocket price, and record every exception so the rules can learn.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Part 3 of this series covered which segments to pursue. Pricing is the next Strategy decision, and in services firms it is usually the least designed. A rate card exists. Proposals are priced by the partner or founder who writes them. Discounts are agreed in the last week of a deal. Nobody can say, at year end, what the firm realised against what it quoted.

A pricing architecture fixes that without making every proposal identical. It sets the rules that most deals follow, the limits within which people can use judgment, and the route for exceptions.

## Price is the largest lever, and the least managed

The case for designing price rests on how far price moves profit. Marn and Rosiello's 1992 analysis in *Harvard Business Review*, using average economics across 2,463 companies, found a 1% improvement in price, with no loss of volume, increased operating profit by 11.1%. The same 1% improvement in volume added about 3.3%, a 1% cut in variable cost about 7.8%, and a 1% cut in fixed cost about 2.3%. The figures are old and the mix of companies was industrial, but the arithmetic holds wherever margins are thin relative to revenue.

More recent work points the same way. McKinsey's 2026 analysis of 140 public distributors found a 1% price increase could lift EBITDA margin by more than 22%, and described a building materials distributor where sales staff were overriding system prices in more than half of all transactions until a pricing architecture cut manual overrides by 80%. Distributors are not services firms. The pattern, discretion without rules leaking margin, is the same.

## What a pricing architecture contains

| Element | The question it answers | What it looks like in a services firm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Value metric | What the client pays for | Days, deliverables, outcomes, a retained capacity, or a mix |
| Fee model | How the fee is structured | Project, retainer, time and materials, success fee or hybrid |
| Packages | Which standard offers exist | Two to four defined scopes with a price each |
| Rate card | What a unit of time or work costs | Rates by role, used for estimating and change requests |
| Discount rules | Who may lower the price, by how much, and why | Approval levels and allowed reasons |
| Scope change terms | What happens when work grows | Change request threshold and pricing method |
| Payment terms | When the money arrives | Deposit, milestones, days to pay, late-payment terms |
| Review rhythm | When the rules are checked against results | Quarterly comparison of quoted, invoiced and collected |

Most firms have the rate card and some packages. The elements that protect realised price (discount rules, scope change terms and the review rhythm) are the ones usually missing.

## Choosing the fee model

The fee model decides who carries risk and what behaviour the fee rewards. Our piece on how marketing services are priced makes the point that the clearest guide to a provider's incentive is what makes its fee go up ([How marketing services are priced](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-services-are-priced/)). The same test applies to a firm pricing its own work.

| Fee model | What it rewards | Who carries estimation risk | Suits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time and materials | Hours worked | The client | Unclear scope, short or exploratory work |
| Fixed project fee | Finishing efficiently | The firm | Defined deliverables with a clear end |
| Retainer | Keeping the relationship | Shared; drifts to the firm if scope grows | Ongoing work with a stable shape |
| Success or outcome fee | The agreed outcome | The firm | Measurable outcomes the firm can influence |
| Hybrid: fixed base plus variable | Both delivery and outcome | Shared | Engagements with a defined core and uncertain upside |

Time-based pricing deserves particular scrutiny. It ties revenue directly to utilisation, and utilisation is under pressure. SPI Research's 2026 Professional Services Maturity Benchmark, published with Deltek, put billable utilisation at 66.4%, its lowest in nearly two decades, against 75% for high-performing firms. Thomson Reuters' 2026 survey of more than 1,500 professionals recorded growing concern that AI may threaten billing models. If AI shortens the hours a task takes, a firm billing by the hour passes the whole gain to the client. A fixed fee or a value metric lets the firm keep part of it. Our piece on seats, usage and outcomes covers the same choice for software ([Seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/)).

## The pocket price: where services firms leak

Marn and Rosiello defined the pocket price as the revenue truly left in a company's pocket from a transaction, after every deduction between list and payment. They called the chart of those deductions the pocket price waterfall. Services firms have their own version.

| Step (illustrative engagement) | Amount | Remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work delivered at rate card: 500 hours at $200 |  | $100,000 |
| Negotiated discount at contract, 10% | −$10,000 | $90,000 |
| Overrun absorbed without a change request: 40 hours | −$8,000 | $82,000 |
| Invoice written off after a dispute | −$2,000 | $80,000 |
| Cost of payment received 90 days late, at 8% a year | −$1,600 | $78,400 |
| Pocket price |  | $78,400, or 78.4% of standard value |

The discount is the line everyone sees. In this example it is less than half the leak. The overrun, the write-off and the slow payment are rarely reported together, because they sit with delivery, finance and the account lead respectively. A pricing architecture puts them on one page.

> The discount is the leak everyone sees. In most services engagements it is less than half of the loss.

## Discount and exception rules

Discounts are not wrong. Undesigned discounts are. Ebsta's 2024 benchmarks, drawn from 4.2 million opportunities, found discounts offered early in a deal were associated with a 39% drop in win rates. Early discounting tends to signal that the price was never firm.

A simple rule set covers most firms.

| Discount or exception | Who approves | Required on the record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Up to 5%, standard terms | The deal owner | Reason from an agreed list |
| 5% to 15%, or a non-standard payment term | Commercial lead | Reason, what the client gives in return, expected outcome |
| Above 15%, a cap on change requests, or a success-only fee | Founder or finance lead | Full rationale, risk to margin, review date |
| Any price for a segment the firm has declined | Commercial lead | Why the exception is worth taking |

Two principles make the rules work. First, every discount should trade for something: a longer term, a faster decision, a case study, a larger scope or prepayment. A discount that buys nothing is a price cut. Second, the allowed reasons should come from a short, fixed list, so exceptions can be compared over a year.

## Recording price decisions so the rules learn

A pricing architecture improves only if its exceptions are graded. That requires the record The Build Order describes: each exception with its reason, approver, status and expected outcome, written back when the outcome is known ([The ten commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)).

After two or three quarters the record answers questions that otherwise run on anecdote. Did discounted proposals win more often than standard ones in each segment? Which reasons predicted renewals? Which clients generated the most absorbed overrun? In Part 10 of The Build Order, a composite distributor found its discounts won no more often than standard quotes in some product lines once the outcomes were recorded ([The same build in four industries](https://lowob.com/research/the-same-build-in-four-industries/)). Services firms usually find something similar.

Pricing for AI-assisted work adds a new question. Software vendors are moving to hybrid structures: Metronome's 2026 review of more than 50 AI pricing models, a vendor catalogue, found most combine subscriptions with usage or credits. Services firms delivering AI-assisted work face the same choice between charging for effort and charging for the result ([What is outcome-based pricing for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-based-pricing-for-ai/)). Whatever they choose, the record makes the effect visible.

Illustrative example: closing the overrun leak

Decision
:   Require a change request for any overrun above 10% of estimated hours, priced at the rate card, before the work is done.

Reason and owner
:   A quarterly comparison of quoted, invoiced and collected fees showed absorbed overruns cost more than negotiated discounts across the year. Owned by the head of delivery; agreed with the commercial lead.

What changed
:   Proposals state the change threshold; project leads log overruns weekly; the pricing review now reports discounts, overruns, write-offs and days to pay on one page.

Illustrative: a composite of a 120-person technical services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Design the rules, not every price.** An architecture sets defaults, limits and an exception route.
- **Measure pocket price.** Discounts, overruns, write-offs and slow payment belong on one page.
- **Choose the fee model by risk and reward.** Hourly billing passes efficiency gains, including AI gains, to the client.
- **Make every discount trade for something.** Record the reason and grade the outcome.

Gateway card

### Before you call it a pricing architecture

- A chosen fee model and value metric for each offer
- Two to four packages with stated scope and price
- Discount approval levels with a fixed list of allowed reasons
- A change request threshold written into every proposal
- A quarterly report of quoted, invoiced and collected fees
- Every exception recorded with an approver and an expected outcome

## Common questions

### What is a pricing architecture?

The set of rules that turns a rate card into the fee a firm keeps: fee model, packages, discount and exception rules, scope change terms, payment terms and a review rhythm.

### How should a professional services firm price its work?

Choose a fee model by who should carry estimation risk and what it rewards, define packages for common scopes, and set discount and change request rules so the realised price stays close to the quoted one.

### What is a pocket price?

The revenue left after every deduction between the list price and payment. For services firms that includes discounts, unbilled overruns, write-offs and the cost of late payment.

### Should services firms stop billing by the hour?

Not always. Hourly billing suits unclear or exploratory work, but it ties revenue to utilisation and passes efficiency gains to the client, so defined work is usually better priced as a fixed fee or by value.

- [Thomson Reuters Institute, 2026 AI in Professional Services Report](https://www.thomsonreuters.com/en/institute/reports/2026-ai-in-professional-services-report). Survey of 1,500+ professionals; attitudes rather than measured pricing change.

Take your last ten completed engagements and build the waterfall for each: standard value, discount, absorbed overrun, write-offs and days to pay. The largest line is where your pricing architecture should start.
